lesson.title: From Shape to Number: Turning Area into Probability
lesson.summary: Area under a density curve between two values equals the proportion or probability of observations falling in that interval, the single fact that makes the normal curve usable for real calculations.
lesson.body:
The uniform spinner example showed that area under a density curve gives the proportion of observations in an interval. That single fact is the entire foundation for using any density curve, including the normal curve, to answer real probability questions. Once you accept that area equals proportion, and proportion of a population equals probability for a randomly selected individual, you have everything you need to turn a bell shaped curve into a working probability calculator, without ever touching a table of raw data.

Because the total area under any density curve equals exactly 1, area gets used two ways. The area to the left of a value x equals the proportion of observations below x, which is exactly what a percentile reports. The area between two values a and b, where a is less than b, equals the proportion of observations between them, and you can find it by subtracting the smaller left tail area from the larger one. This subtraction trick, area up to b minus area up to a, is how nearly every normal curve probability problem actually gets solved.

One subtlety trips up many students: for a continuous distribution, the area above a single exact point is zero, because a single point has zero width, and area requires both a width and a height. This means the probability that X equals exactly 500, for a continuous variable, is technically zero, and it is why the probability of X being less than 500 equals the probability of X being less than or equal to 500 for continuous data, unlike with counts or other discrete outcomes.

The normal density curve gives the cleanest illustration of area in action. Precise calculation shows that the area between one standard deviation below and one above the mean is 0.6827, between two standard deviations it is 0.9545, and between three it is 0.9973, the exact values behind the rounded 68, 95, 99.7 empirical rule. Because a normal curve is symmetric, the total area of 1 splits evenly at the mean, so the area to the right of the mean is exactly 0.5. Combine these two facts to find the area between the mean and one standard deviation above it: since the area from one standard deviation below to one above is 0.6827, and that region splits evenly around the mean by symmetry, the area from the mean up to one standard deviation above it is 0.6827 divided by 2, which equals 0.34135, or about 34.1 percent.

Every calculation you will do with the normal distribution, whether by hand with a table or with technology, is really just this same area idea applied to whatever mean and standard deviation the problem gives you. The next step is learning to compute these areas, and their inverses, quickly and precisely using a calculator or software, but the underlying logic never changes: a probability is an area, and an area is what you get by measuring the region under the curve between two boundaries.
